rules.statement: A serialization API writes its output to a caller-supplied IBufferWriter<byte> or Utf8JsonWriter instead of returning a newly allocated byte[].
rules.why: Returning a byte[] breaks the buffer convention and allocates an array for every call. Writing to a buffer writer lets callers use pooled buffers.
rules.check: Look for new public or internal methods that serialize to bytes and return byte[] (for example SerializeToUtf8Bytes or ToArray results) where a buffer-writer overload could be used instead.

rules.statement: Methods that produce bytes into a buffer writer take the destination as a generic `ref TWriter destination` parameter constrained `where TWriter : IBufferWriter<byte>, allows ref struct`, so ref struct writers are accepted.
rules.why: This is the standard producer shape. It lets callers pass stack-only, ref struct buffer writers without boxing.
rules.check: Look for new methods that take a plain `IBufferWriter<byte>` output parameter when the generic `ref TWriter ... allows ref struct` form would work. When the plain form is needed, for example to feed a Utf8JsonWriter, the reason should be documented.

rules.statement: Put the input or source parameter first and the output destination (writer, buffer writer, destination span) last in a method signature.
rules.why: It keeps signatures consistent with the existing source-first, destination-last APIs such as Decode(ciphertext, ref destination) and CopyPlaintext(source, destination).
rules.check: Look for new methods whose first parameter is a Utf8JsonWriter, IBufferWriter, destination span or other output, placed before the input being processed.

rules.statement: Parse JSON with JsonElement.Parse instead of JsonDocument.Parse in new code.
rules.why: The maintainer wants to stop using the older JsonDocument parsing APIs. JsonElement.Parse returns a value with no document to own and dispose.
rules.check: Look for newly added JsonDocument.Parse (or JsonDocument usage generally) in production or test code where JsonElement.Parse would do.

rules.statement: Read endpoint information (such as the endpoint name) from HttpContext, for example via HttpContext.GetEndpoint() and IEndpointNameMetadata, instead of passing it as a separate parameter next to the HttpContext.
rules.why: The HttpContext already carries the endpoint metadata, so a separate parameter is redundant and can disagree with it.
rules.check: Look for methods that take both an HttpContext and an endpoint name or endpoint argument that could be derived from httpContext.GetEndpoint().
